misfits.thing: Asphalt road surface
misfits.where: Center and foreground of the image, covering the whole street
misfits.why: Smooth dark asphalt is a modern paving material and would not exist in a village around 1350, which would have had dirt, cobbles, or packed earth tracks.

misfits.thing: White dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Down the center of the road, running from the foreground into the distance
misfits.why: Painted road lane markings are a modern traffic convention and did not exist in medieval Bohemia.

misfits.thing: Smooth grey asphalt road surface
misfits.where: Center and foreground of the image, running from the bottom edge up to the village in the distance
misfits.why: Asphalt paving is a modern road-building material; a 1350 village street would be dirt, gravel, or cobbles.

misfits.thing: White painted dashed and solid lane markings
misfits.where: Down the middle of the road in the foreground and midground
misfits.why: Painted traffic lane lines are a modern road feature and did not exist around 1350.

misfits.thing: Asphalt paved road
misfits.where: Center and right foreground, covering the whole street
misfits.why: Modern asphalt paving did not exist in 1350; the street would have been dirt, mud, or cobblestone.

misfits.thing: White dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Painted down the middle of the asphalt road
misfits.why: Painted traffic lane lines are a modern road feature and have no place in a medieval village.

misfits.thing: Red brick chimneys
misfits.where: Top left corner above the first thatched roof, and on the right-side cottages at upper right
misfits.why: Brick chimneys of this neat modern form are unlikely on 1350 peasant thatched cottages, which were typically smoke-vented through the roof or had simple hearths.

misfits.thing: Paved asphalt road with white dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Center and right of the image, running through the village street
misfits.why: Modern asphalt paving and painted lane markings did not exist around 1350; a medieval village street would be dirt, mud, or cobbled.

misfits.thing: Asphalt road surface with painted white lane markings
misfits.where: Center of the image, running from the foreground up to the village in the distance
misfits.why: Smooth black asphalt paving and painted dashed and solid white lane lines are modern road features. Around 1350 village streets would have been dirt, mud, or cobbles, not asphalt with traffic markings.

misfits.thing: Paved asphalt road with white dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Center and right of the image, running through the village street
misfits.why: Asphalt paving and painted lane markings are modern road features that did not exist in a village around 1350.

misfits.thing: Street lamp with a metal pole and a glowing electric-style bulb under a dome shade
misfits.where: Right edge of the image, along the sidewalk curb beside the shop entrance
misfits.why: Street lighting like this, with a metal pole and a bulb-style lamp, is a modern invention. Romans of the 1st century AD had no electric lamps and used oil lamps or torches at most.

misfits.thing: Modern metal street lamp with a glass-shade light fixture
misfits.where: Right side of the street, rising from the sidewalk edge beside the shop front
misfits.why: Electric-style street lighting with a metal pole and lamp housing is a modern invention and did not exist in 1st-century Roman streets, which were lit by oil lamps or torches.

misfits.thing: Black metal street lamp with a glowing electric-style bulb
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the sidewalk beside the amphora and extending over the street at upper right
misfits.why: Its curved modern cast-iron design and bright bulb look like a later electric or gas-era street light, not an ancient Roman oil lamp or torch bracket.

misfits.thing: Modern metal street lamp with a glowing lamp head
misfits.where: Right side of the image, along the sidewalk edge next to the shop front
misfits.why: Electric-style streetlight with a metal pole and enclosed lamp fixture does not belong to a 1st century AD Roman street, which would have been lit by oil lamps or torches.

misfits.thing: Street lamp
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the pavement beside the shop doorway and amphora, with a glowing lamp head at the top
misfits.why: The tall black metal pole and enclosed electric-style lamp fixture are modern. A 1st-century Roman street would have lit its way with oil lamps or torches, not a metal lamp post.

misfits.thing: Modern street lamp with glowing electric-style bulb
misfits.where: Right side of the image, on the sidewalk near the building corner
misfits.why: Metal lamp post with a dome-shaped fixture and bright bulb is a modern streetlight design; 1st-century Roman streets were not lit by such fixtures.

misfits.thing: Metal street lamp base and pole
misfits.where: Right foreground, rising from the curb
misfits.why: Cast-iron/steel pole and circular base are modern municipal street furniture, not Roman.

misfits.thing: Hanging glass-walled lantern with an open flame
misfits.where: Upper left, hanging from the iron wall bracket beside the shop doorway
misfits.why: The enclosed glass-paneled lantern style looks more medieval or modern than the terracotta or bronze oil lamps typical of 1st-century Roman streets.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane glazed window with a wooden grid frame
misfits.where: Right side of the house wall, behind the seated woman and man
misfits.why: Large glass-paned windows were not used in Viking Age houses around 900; openings were typically unglazed or covered with shutters or cloth.

misfits.thing: Window with multi-pane glass
misfits.where: Right side of the back wall, beside the shields, showing a view of mountains and a lake
misfits.why: Window glass was not in common use in Scandinavian houses around 900 AD. Such a window would have been an open shutter or a covered opening, not a paned glass window.

misfits.thing: Knitting with needles
misfits.where: The woman seated on the bench at right, holding a pale knitted piece in her lap
misfits.why: Knitting with two needles did not reach Scandinavia until much later. Viking-age textile work used nalbinding or weaving, so this craft is anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Window with a multi-pane grid frame and clear glass-like panes
misfits.where: Right wall, beside the seated woman with the spear
misfits.why: Window glass was not used in Viking-age longhouses around 900; openings were typically unglazed shutters or smoke holes, so a glazed window is anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a white-framed glass grid
misfits.where: Center-right of the back wall, between the two shields, above the seated family
misfits.why: Glazed windows with framed panes were not used in Viking-age houses around 900; openings were covered with shutters or hides, so this window looks anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a grid of glazing bars
misfits.where: Center-right of the image, in the wooden wall between the shield and the seated family
misfits.why: Window glass was not available in Viking Age longhouses around 900; openings were typically unglazed shutters or covered with cloth or hide.

misfits.thing: Glazed skylight opening in the roof
misfits.where: Top of the image, in the ceiling above the hearth
misfits.why: The framed roof opening appears to have glass or a pane set into it, which would be anachronistic for a Viking Age longhouse; smoke holes were open or covered only by simple wooden or hide coverings.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a grid of small rectangular panes
misfits.where: Center-right wall, behind the man and children, showing a snowy view outside
misfits.why: Glazed, multi-pane windows like this are a later medieval or modern feature. Around 900 AD a Viking longhouse would have had at most a small wooden shutter or an open vent, not a paned window.

misfits.thing: Striped, geometric-patterned flatweave rug
misfits.where: Bottom right corner of the floor, in front of the bench
misfits.why: The bright, bold, multi-band geometric pattern resembles later kilim or modern rug designs more than the simpler textiles and furs typical of Viking-age floors.

misfits.thing: Glass skylight with a metal frame in the roof
misfits.where: Top center of the image, cut into the roof above the smoke
misfits.why: Glass panes set in a metal-framed roof opening are a modern construction feature; a Viking longhouse around 900 would have had only smoke holes or wooden openings.

misfits.thing: Rectangular skylight opening in the roof
misfits.where: Top-left corner of the ceiling, above the hanging cauldron
misfits.why: It looks like a glazed or pane-like opening with a flat, pale blue surface, and window glass was rare in Viking-age houses, which used open smoke holes or shuttered openings.

misfits.thing: blue plastic bucket with a molded handle
misfits.where: right side of the yard, beside the man's legs, near the bottom right of the central figure
misfits.why: Molded plastic buckets are a 20th-century product. A mid-1800s farm would use wooden, tin, or iron buckets.

misfits.thing: Bright blue bucket with a molded plastic look
misfits.where: Held in the farmer's right hand, at his side near his legs
misfits.why: The glossy, uniformly colored blue bucket looks like modern plastic or painted metal rather than a 1850s wooden, tin, or galvanized pail.

misfits.thing: Blue plastic bucket with a wire handle
misfits.where: Held in the man's right hand at the right side of the image, roughly center-right, near the bottom of his figure
misfits.why: Brightly colored molded plastic was not available in the 1850s; farm buckets of that era were made of wood, tin, or galvanized iron.

misfits.thing: blue plastic bucket
misfits.where: right side of the yard, beside the man's legs, around the middle-right of the image
misfits.why: Brightly colored molded plastic was not available in the 1850s; buckets of that period were made of wood, metal, or leather.

misfits.thing: bright blue plastic bucket
misfits.where: lower left, beside the man's boots on the dirt
misfits.why: Molded plastic buckets in this saturated blue were not made until well after the 1850s; a period farmyard would use a wooden, tin, or galvanized metal pail.

misfits.thing: blue plastic bucket
misfits.where: center-right of the dirt yard, beside the man and near the fence line
misfits.why: Its smooth molded plastic look and bright blue color are modern; a farmyard in the 1850s would use wooden or metal buckets, like the wooden bucket the man is holding.

misfits.thing: Yellow plastic ear tag on the cow's ear
misfits.where: On the brown-and-white cow at the left edge, in its visible ear near the head
misfits.why: Modern livestock identification ear tags were not used on farms in the 1850s, so this item is anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Black dome pendant lamp with a glowing electric-style bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at the top center of the image
misfits.why: Its industrial dome shade and bulb look like a modern electric light fixture, which does not fit a medieval monastery scriptorium that would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Dark metal industrial-style pendant ceiling lamp with a light bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at the top center of the room
misfits.why: Its modern shape and electric bulb do not fit a medieval monastery scriptorium, which would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Hanging pendant lamp with a dark metal dome shade and a clear glass light bulb
misfits.where: Top center of the image, suspended from the wooden ceiling beams
misfits.why: A modern electric light fixture with a glass bulb does not belong in a medieval monastery scriptorium, which would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: black metal pendant ceiling lamp with a glowing electric-style bulb
misfits.where: hanging from the vaulted ceiling at the top center of the room
misfits.why: Electric-style pendant lamps and bulbs are a modern invention; a medieval scriptorium would be lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Pendant ceiling lamp with a glowing light bulb
misfits.where: Top center of the room, hanging from the wooden ceiling above the central work area
misfits.why: The metal conical shade and glowing incandescent bulb are modern electric lighting; a medieval scriptorium would be lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight from the windows.

misfits.thing: Electric light bulb with metal pendant shade
misfits.where: Hanging from the wooden ceiling at the top center of the image
misfits.why: Electric incandescent bulbs and pendant fixtures are a modern invention; a medieval scriptorium would be lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Clear plastic water bottle with blue cap
misfits.where: Center-right of the forest floor, lying among the fallen leaves
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: Clear plastic water bottle with blue screw cap
misfits.where: Right side of the image, lying on the leaf litter in the middle-right foreground
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: Clear plastic water bottle with blue cap

misfits.where: center-right foreground, lying on the leaf litter below the mushroom cluster
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural autumn beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: Clear plastic water bottle with blue cap
misfits.where: Center-right foreground, lying on the leaf litter below the mossy trunk
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural, undisturbed beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: clear plastic water bottle with blue screw cap
misfits.where: lower right of the leaf-covered forest floor, lying on its side among the leaves

misfits.thing: Pine cone
misfits.where: Right side of the image, on the leaf litter in front of the mossy root
misfits.why: It is a conifer cone, but the scene is a pure beech forest with no conifers visible, so it is a plant part from a different forest type.

misfits.thing: Steel electricity pylon with power lines
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the meadow edge across the mid-ground toward the mountains
misfits.why: Man-made utility infrastructure intrudes on the pastoral alpine nature scene, though power pylons are modern and do exist in real alpine valleys, so it is a modern feature rather than a wrong-period object; it is a common intrusion in nature scenes.

misfits.thing: Steel electricity pylon with power lines
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the meadow near the middle-right background
misfits.why: A modern high-voltage transmission tower is man-made infrastructure that is out of place in a pristine alpine meadow nature scene, though it is plausibly present-day rather than from the wrong period.

misfits.thing: Steel lattice electricity pylon with power lines
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the meadow near the right edge and stretching lines across the sky and mountains
misfits.why: Industrial power infrastructure is man-made and does not belong in a pristine alpine meadow nature scene, though it is present-day, so it is a modern intrusion rather than a period mismatch.

misfits.thing: Corrugated blue metal roof
misfits.where: Top of the warehouse building on the right, spanning the full width of the structure
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern material and did not exist in ancient Egypt around 1400 BC, when roofs were flat mud-brick or timber with reed or palm-frond covering.

misfits.thing: Burlap-style sacks with tied tops
misfits.where: Stacked on the quay near the warehouse, on the cart, and in the foreground boat
misfits.why: The sacks look like modern woven jute or burlap bags. Ancient Egyptians stored grain in woven baskets, reed bins, and clay or pottery jars, so these sacks look anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof
misfits.where: Top of the storehouse building on the right side of the quay
misfits.why: Corrugated metal roofing is a modern material. Ancient Egyptian storehouses had flat or gently sloped roofs of mud brick, timber, and reed matting.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof
misfits.where: Top of the mudbrick warehouse on the right side of the quay
misfits.why: Corrugated metal sheeting is a modern roofing material; ancient Egyptian storehouses would have had flat mud-brick or timber-and-reed roofs.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof on the storehouse
misfits.where: Top of the mud-brick storehouse building on the right side of the quay
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern material and did not exist in ancient Egypt around 1400 BC, which used mud-brick, wood, and reed roofing.

misfits.thing: Metal chain linking the mooring posts
misfits.where: Between the wooden mooring posts along the quay edge, above the lower reed boat
misfits.why: Chain of this form is a later metalwork technology; Bronze Age Egyptian mooring would use rope or plaited fiber lines.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal sheet roof
misfits.where: Covering the mud-brick storehouse on the right side of the image
misfits.why: Ribbed sheet metal is a modern roofing material. Around 1400 BC Egyptian buildings had flat or gabled roofs of palm-wood beams, reeds, and mud, not corrugated metal.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof sheeting
misfits.where: Top of the mudbrick storehouse on the right side of the quay
misfits.why: Corrugated galvanized metal is a modern material and did not exist in Bronze Age Egypt around 1400 BC, which had flat or thatched/palm-wood roofs.

misfits.thing: Chain (metal-looking links) hanging in a sag between the wooden bollards along the quay wall
misfits.where: Center-right of the image, stretching from the bollard at the middle down to the bollard at the right edge of the quay wall
misfits.why: Metal chains were not used for mooring in ancient Egypt around 1400 BC; boats were tied with plant-fiber or leather rope.

misfits.thing: Stacked grain sacks with a coarse burlap-like weave
misfits.where: Right side of the quay, piled against the warehouse wall
misfits.why: Their texture and stacking resemble modern jute or burlap sacks rather than ancient Egyptian storage, which used baskets, jars, and woven mats.

misfits.thing: Triangular lateen-style sail on the distant boat
misfits.where: Middle distance on the river, center-left of the image
misfits.why: The sharp triangular sail resembles later Mediterranean or Arabian lateen rigs. Egyptian sails of around 1400 BC were typically square.
